theory.intro: When angles sit side by side along a straight line, they fill a half turn, so together they add to $180^{\circ}$. These are called **supplementary** angles.
facts: A straight line is a half turn, which measures $180^{\circ}$.
If one angle is known, subtract it from $180^{\circ}$ to find the other.
steps: Check the angles sit along a straight line (a half turn).

workedExamples.solution_text:
Angles on a straight line add to $180^{\circ}$.
$\begin{aligned}x+112^{\circ}&=180^{\circ}\\x&=180^{\circ}-112^{\circ}\\x&=68^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

Angles on a straight line add to $180^{\circ}$.
$\begin{aligned}y+32.5^{\circ}+46.75^{\circ}&=180^{\circ}\\y+79.25^{\circ}&=180^{\circ}\\y&=100.75^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

Subtract the known angle from $180^{\circ}$ because the two angles fill a straight angle.
$\begin{aligned}a+146^{\circ}&=180^{\circ}\\a&=180^{\circ}-146^{\circ}\\a&=34^{\circ}\end{aligned}$

$137^{\circ}+45^{\circ}=182^{\circ}$.
Angles on one side of a straight line must total $180^{\circ}$, so $PQR$ cannot be straight.

Noah says the unknown is $180+143=323^{\circ}$.
Correct his method.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large},scale=0.9]\usetikzlibrary{angles,quotes}\coordinate (O) at (0,0);\coordinate (A) at (2.5,0);\coordinate (B) at (-2.5,0);\coordinate (C) at (143:2.2);\draw (B)--(A);\draw (O)--(C);\pic[draw,"$143^{\circ}$",angle radius=0.65cm,angle eccentricity=1.8]{angle=A--O--C};\pic[draw,"$x$",angle radius=0.9cm,angle eccentricity=1.7]{angle=C--O--B};\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
development.solution_text:
$143^{\circ}+x=180^{\circ}$
$x=180^{\circ}-143^{\circ}$
$=37^{\circ}$
The known angle must be subtracted from the half-turn total.
